questions.prompt:
Written scenario data: The taxiway sign assembly has a black location panel displaying A and a yellow direction panel with a left arrow toward B.

The written scenario data describe a combined airport sign assembly. Which interpretation matches the assembly?

choices.A: Both panels grant clearance to cross the next runway.
choices.B: You are on Taxiway B, and Taxiway A is indicated to the left.
choices.C: You are on Taxiway A, and Taxiway B is indicated to the left.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: The black location panel identifies the current taxiway A. The yellow direction panel points left toward B.
Why A is incorrect: Location and direction signs provide information. They do not themselves grant a runway-crossing clearance.
Why B is incorrect: That exchanges the functions and letters of the two panels.
Reference: FAA AIM, §2-3-6, Other Markings — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap2_section_3.html
Reference: FAA AIM, Chapter 2, Aeronautical Lighting and Other Airport Visual Aids — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap2_section_1.html

questions.prompt: A drone has an ATC transponder. With no specific FAA authorization, the crew proposes turning it on for the flight so radar operators can identify the aircraft. What does §107.52 require?

choices.A: Turn it on if the aircraft's Remote ID is also operating.
choices.B: Turn it on whenever the drone is outside Class G.
choices.C: Keep the transponder off unless the Administrator authorizes its use.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Section 107.52 prohibits operating the small UAS with a transponder on unless otherwise authorized by the Administrator.
Why A is incorrect: Remote ID compliance does not authorize turning on an ATC transponder.
Why B is incorrect: An airspace class does not by itself supply the required authorization.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.52 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.52

questions.prompt: A qualified current pilot is assigned a drone whose aircraft registration has been revoked. The plastic pilot certificate and aircraft hardware are both in good condition. What prevents the proposed ordinary flight?

choices.A: Only a lack of pilot knowledge recency could prevent it.
choices.B: The revoked registration remains effective until its printed expiration date.
choices.C: The aircraft lacks effective registration.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Effective aircraft registration is independent of pilot qualifications and the hardware's condition. A revoked registration cannot be relied on until resolved.
Why A is incorrect: Current pilot knowledge does not establish the aircraft's registration status.
Why B is incorrect: A revocation changes effectiveness independently of a later printed expiry.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.13 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.13
Reference: 14 CFR § 48.100 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-48/section-48.100

questions.prompt: A proposed broadcast-module substitute uploads identification data to a website using cellular service. It sends no required local Remote ID radio broadcast. Does access to the website alone satisfy the module pathway?

choices.A: Yes. Any website showing the serial number counts as the module broadcast.
choices.B: No. Internet availability does not replace the required compliant Remote ID broadcast.
choices.C: Yes. A cellular subscription automatically supplies the non-proprietary broadcast specification.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: The module pathway requires the specified compliant broadcast equipment and functionality. A cloud-only feed does not supply that radio broadcast.
Why A is incorrect: Displaying some information online is different from broadcasting the required elements under the specified requirements.
Why C is incorrect: A communications subscription does not establish the required Remote ID broadcast implementation.
Reference: 14 CFR § 89.115 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-89/section-89.115
Reference: 14 CFR § 89.320 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-89/section-89.320

questions.prompt: A warmly dressed pilot develops numb fingers and cannot reliably distinguish small control inputs during the ground check. What needs to be resolved?

choices.A: Proceed because the pilot's torso feels warm.
choices.B: Launch and use turbulence to check whether finger sensitivity returns.
choices.C: Restore reliable control ability or assign a suitable qualified pilot before flight.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Reliable control is a functional requirement for safe operation. Overall comfort does not establish fine-motor ability.
Why A is incorrect: Warm clothing does not rule out impaired hand function.
Why B is incorrect: An airborne trial introduces risk while the control problem remains unresolved.
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt:
Written scenario data: The chart's Sedona airport lighting entry shows an asterisk before L, indicating that the lighting entry has special information or limitations documented elsewhere.

The Sedona airport data include an asterisk before the lighting entry L. What planning action does that symbol support?

choices.A: Check the Chart Supplement for lighting limitations or special information.
choices.B: Treat the asterisk as permission for all drone night flights nearby.
choices.C: Assume the airport has no lights under any circumstances.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The asterisk indicates lighting limitations or special information. The Chart Supplement supplies the applicable details.
Why B is incorrect: An airport lighting annotation does not grant drone operating permission.
Why C is incorrect: A qualified lighting entry is different from an airport with no lighting entry.
Reference: FAA Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide, July 9, 2026, VFR Terms and Symbols — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav/digital_products/aero_guide/
Reference: FAA, Chart Supplements — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav/digital_products/dafd/
Reference: FAA VFR Raster Charts, Sectionals and effective dates — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav/digital_products/vfr/

questions.prompt: After moving, a remote pilot notifies the FAA of the new permanent mailing address within 30 days. The effective pilot certificate still shows the old address. Does §107.77(b) require the pilot to wait for a corrected printed certificate solely because the printing is old?

choices.A: Yes. Every residential move automatically cancels the pilot certificate.
choices.B: Yes. The notification has no effect until a replacement is physically delivered.
choices.C: No. The section's address-notification condition has been met.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Section 107.77(b) limits exercising privileges after 30 days unless the FAA has been notified. On these facts that notification was made.
Why A is incorrect: Moving does not automatically cancel the certificate under this section.
Why B is incorrect: The provision does not make receipt of a newly printed certificate the notification trigger.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.77 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.77

questions.prompt:
Written scenario data: The METAR gives temperature group M03/M05, with M denoting a negative Celsius value.

What temperature-dew point spread should the crew enter in its weather notes?
questions.explanation:
Why B works: M03 means −3°C and M05 means −5°C. The spread is −3 − (−5) = 2°C.
Why A is incorrect: Adding the magnitudes ignores their signed values and does not compute the spread.
Why C is incorrect: Temperature is 2°C above dew point rather than 2°C below it.
Reference: FAA-H-8083-28B, Aviation Weather Handbook — https://www.faa.gov/regulationspolicies/handbooksmanuals/aviation/faa-h-8083-28b-aviation-weather-handbook
Reference: NOAA Aviation Weather Center, Aviation Weather Data Help, TAF — https://aviationweather.gov/help/data/

questions.prompt: A crew appoints a visual observer who will not manipulate controls or act as remote PIC. What does Part 107 require regarding that observer's remote pilot certificate?

choices.A: The observer must pass UAG even if no pilot certificate is issued.
choices.B: Every visual observer must hold the same pilot certificate as the remote PIC.
choices.C: The observer does not need that certificate solely to serve as visual observer.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Part 107 specifies duties for the observer, but it does not require a remote pilot certificate just for that role.
Why A is incorrect: A separate UAG pass is not a stated qualification for the observer role.
Why B is incorrect: The certificate requirement for the remote PIC does not automatically extend to the observer.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.12 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.12
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.33 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.33
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt: A second crew member opens a video window labeled REPLAY and reports that the aircraft has cleared a roof. The pilot's direct observation shows it has not. What should the crew do?

choices.A: Treat the replay as historical, correct the report, and use current verified observations for control.
choices.B: Use the replay position until the direct view agrees with it.
choices.C: Treat every video window as live because the controller is still connected.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: A replay depicts an earlier recorded state. The label and conflicting current observation identify a report that cannot establish present clearance.
Why B is incorrect: The historical view should not override verified current aircraft position.
Why C is incorrect: An active connection does not make every window a live stream.
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak

questions.prompt: During UAG, a candidate copies an actual test item onto a card and intentionally removes the card to study privately. The candidate does not share it or change an answer. Is the lack of sharing or answer changes a defense under §107.69(a)(1)?

choices.A: No. Copying or intentionally removing knowledge-test material is separately prohibited.
choices.B: Yes. Unauthorized conduct requires a changed exam score.
choices.C: Yes. The prohibition applies only when another candidate receives the material.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: Section 107.69(a)(1) prohibits copying or intentionally removing a knowledge test. Sharing and changes to answers are not conditions of that prohibition.
Why B is incorrect: The copying and removal prohibition does not depend on proving a score change.
Why C is incorrect: Giving material to another applicant is a separate prohibited act.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.69 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.69

questions.prompt: An ordinary commercial landlord owns a suitable field but is neither a recognized community-based organization nor an educational institution. Does ownership alone make the landlord eligible to apply for a FRIA?

choices.A: Yes. Any holder of a remote pilot certificate is an eligible FRIA applicant.
choices.B: No. The applicant must meet the eligibility categories in §89.205.
choices.C: Yes. Any landowner is an eligible FRIA applicant.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: Section 89.205 identifies recognized community-based organizations and educational institutions as eligible applicants. Field ownership alone does not meet that condition.
Why A is incorrect: A remote pilot certificate does not itself create an eligible applicant organization.
Why C is incorrect: Ownership is different from the applicant eligibility the section specifies.
Reference: 14 CFR § 89.205 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-89/section-89.205

questions.prompt: A training chart gives a true outbound course of 070° and a 12° west magnetic variation. Use magnetic course = true course + west variation. What is the magnetic course for the reciprocal return leg?
questions.explanation:
Why A works: The true reciprocal is 070° + 180° = 250°. Adding 12° west variation gives 262° magnetic.
Why B is incorrect: 238° subtracts the west variation instead of using the stated addition rule.
Why C is incorrect: 250° is the true return course before applying variation.
Reference: FAA Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide, July 9, 2026, VFR Terms and Symbols — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav/digital_products/aero_guide/
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, ch. 16, Navigation — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak

questions.prompt: A radio reply says “Stand by.” What does the sender expect the recipient to do?

choices.A: Assume every requested action has been approved.
choices.B: Wait while the sender is occupied and expects to call again.
choices.C: Repeat the full message continuously until interrupted.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: Stand by asks the recipient to pause, generally because the sender or receiver is occupied, and a later call is expected.
Why A is incorrect: The phrase is not an approval of the requested action.
Why C is incorrect: Repeated transmissions would defeat the request to wait and could occupy the frequency.
Reference: FAA AIM, §4-2, Radio Communications Phraseology and Techniques — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap4_section_2.html
Reference: FAA Pilot/Controller Glossary, STAND BY — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/pcg_html/glossary-s.html

questions.prompt: A drone's anti-collision light is visible at the required range. At the control station, however, prominent lighted ground references can be identified only 2 statute miles away. Does the aircraft light alone establish the required nighttime flight visibility?

choices.A: Yes. The light replaces the requirement to see surrounding references.
choices.B: Yes. Nighttime flight visibility is measured only from the drone's camera.
choices.C: No. The observed flight visibility is a separate requirement from the light's visibility range.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Section 107.51(c) specifies flight visibility observed from the control station using prominent references. Section 107.29 supplies a separate lighting requirement.
Why A is incorrect: Seeing the aircraft light does not establish the visibility of surrounding references.
Why B is incorrect: The camera is not the specified observation location for this minimum.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.29 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.29
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.51 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.51

questions.prompt: Warm moist air moves over much colder coastal water toward a launch site during the afternoon. Visibility deteriorates even though the wind continues and the sun is up. Which mechanism best explains the fog risk?

choices.A: Radiation fog that can form only after the wind and sunlight both stop.
choices.B: Advection cooling of the moving moist air over the cold surface.
choices.C: Compression warming of air descending over the cold water.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: Moving moist air can cool to saturation over a colder surface and form advection fog. The process does not require night or calm conditions.
Why A is incorrect: Radiation fog depends on surface radiational cooling and is not the mechanism described by this moving warm-moist-air setup.
Why C is incorrect: Compression warming moves air away from saturation rather than explaining this cooling mechanism.
Reference: FAA-H-8083-28B, Aviation Weather Handbook — https://www.faa.gov/regulationspolicies/handbooksmanuals/aviation/faa-h-8083-28b-aviation-weather-handbook

questions.prompt: A Part 107 crew has the required prior ATC authorization for its Class D flight. The issued terms add no radio-carriage condition. Does §107.41 itself require every such drone to carry a two-way aviation radio?

choices.A: Yes. An aviation handheld radio automatically serves as the airspace authorization.
choices.B: No. The section requires prior authorization and does not itself impose a universal radio-carriage requirement.
choices.C: Yes. The aircraft must always have an onboard two-way aviation radio.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: The crew must meet the issued authorization and other applicable requirements. Section 107.41 itself establishes the prior-authorization requirement rather than universal radio carriage.
Why A is incorrect: Possessing communication equipment does not constitute ATC authorization.
Why C is incorrect: The section does not state that equipment requirement for every drone.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.41 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.41
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt: A visual observer can still see the aircraft after a concrete mixer parks between the observer and pilot. The crew's voice calls are now unintelligible and no working alternate communication method is available. What must be resolved?

choices.A: Restore effective communication or safely change the crew arrangement before relying on that observer.
choices.B: Only the drone's registration needs to be checked again.
choices.C: Nothing, because visual contact with the drone satisfies every observer requirement.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: Section 107.33 requires effective communication at all times when an observer is used. Continued visual contact does not resolve the communication failure.
Why B is incorrect: Registration status does not repair the failed crew communication path.
Why C is incorrect: The visual and communication duties are separate.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.33 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.33

questions.prompt: A newly assigned launch assistant attended a meeting covering weather, normal roles, and the route. The meeting omitted emergency and contingency procedures. Has attendance alone established the required preflight briefing for that assistant?

choices.A: Yes. Ground participants need only the weather portion.
choices.B: Yes. Physical attendance satisfies the rule regardless of the information presented.
choices.C: No. The assistant must also be informed about the required emergency and contingency procedures.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Section 107.49(b) specifies the information that all direct participants must receive. Attendance is not a substitute for omitted required content.
Why A is incorrect: Direct ground participants are included in the specified briefing duty.
Why B is incorrect: A meeting can take place without communicating every required subject.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.49 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.49

questions.prompt:
Written scenario data: The battery's maximum cell voltage is 4.15 V and minimum is 3.88 V. The acceptance criterion permits no more than 0.10 V spread.

The fictional battery procedure permits no more than 0.10 volt between the highest and lowest cells. in the written scenario data, what should the crew record?

choices.A: A 0.27-volt spread, which fails the stated check despite the plausible pack total.
choices.B: A 0.01-volt spread, because only the two highest cells are compared.
choices.C: A pass based solely on the 16.32-volt total.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The highest cell is 4.15 volts and the lowest is 3.88 volts. Their difference is 0.27 volt, above 0.10.
Why B is incorrect: The criterion compares the maximum and minimum across all cells, including the low cell.
Why C is incorrect: A total can appear plausible while individual cells are substantially unbalanced.
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, ch. 11, Aircraft Performance — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak

questions.prompt: A drone starts at 180 feet AGL and climbs to 360 feet AGL over level ground. A uniform cloud base is 800 feet AGL directly overhead. No waiver applies. What is the highest height on this climb that satisfies the 500-foot-below-cloud requirement?

choices.A: 360 feet AGL.
choices.B: 400 feet AGL.
choices.C: 300 feet AGL.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Subtract the required 500 feet from the 800-foot cloud base to obtain 300 feet AGL. The climb would lose the required clearance above that height.
Why A is incorrect: At 360 feet AGL, only 440 feet of clearance remains.
Why B is incorrect: The general 400-foot altitude limit does not ensure a separate 500-foot cloud margin.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.51 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.51

questions.prompt: A standard Remote ID test demonstrates 95-percent geometric-altitude accuracy within 20 feet for the control station and within 100 feet for the aircraft. Considering only these two accuracy limits, what fails?

choices.A: The control-station result fails its 15-foot limit, while the aircraft result meets its 150-foot limit.
choices.B: Both pass because both errors are under 150 feet.
choices.C: The aircraft fails because every geometric altitude must be accurate within 15 feet.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: Section 89.310(h) specifies different tolerances. Twenty exceeds the control station's 15-foot tolerance. One hundred is within the aircraft's 150-foot tolerance.
Why B is incorrect: The aircraft's tolerance is not the control station's tolerance.
Why C is incorrect: The aircraft altitude has its own 150-foot limit at the specified probability.
Reference: 14 CFR § 89.310 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-89/section-89.310

questions.prompt: A company attempts to list one broadcast module's serial number on two separate active Part 107 aircraft registration certificates at the same time. The module will be physically moved between drones rather than flown twice at once. Is simultaneous listing allowed under §48.110(a)(7)?

choices.A: No. That module serial number must not be listed on more than one aircraft registration certificate at the same time.
choices.B: Yes. Physical movement of the module makes duplicate active listings permissible.
choices.C: Yes. A company may use any one module serial number for its whole Part 107 fleet.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The section expressly prohibits listing the module serial number on more than one registration certificate simultaneously. A planned physical swap does not remove that record requirement.
Why B is incorrect: Not using the module on both flights at once is different from its simultaneous registration listing.
Why C is incorrect: Separate Part 107 aircraft records do not become one certificate because the owner is the same.
Reference: 14 CFR § 48.110 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-48/section-48.110
Reference: 14 CFR § 89.115 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-89/section-89.115

questions.prompt: An observer sees intermittent flashes near a parked aircraft and reports that it is moving. A rotating airport beacon sweeps through the same view. What information best helps resolve the report?

choices.A: An assumption that every flashing light belongs to an airborne aircraft.
choices.B: The number of flashes alone, without checking the aircraft's position.
choices.C: The aircraft's position relative to stable nearby references across successive observations.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Independent positional references help distinguish actual movement from changing illumination.
Why A is incorrect: Beacons, vehicles, and parked equipment can produce or reflect flashing light.
Why B is incorrect: A flash count does not show displacement of the aircraft.
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA AIM, §8-1-6, Vision in Flight — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap8_section_1.html

questions.prompt: A Category 4 aircraft's approved operating limitations permit the intended over-people operation only in daylight. The client reschedules it to night and provides compliant anti-collision lighting. Is that lighting alone enough to use the same Category 4 plan?

choices.A: Yes. Meeting §107.29 automatically changes the approved aircraft limitations.
choices.B: No. The aircraft's daylight operating limitation must also be satisfied.
choices.C: Yes. Category 4 status removes every daylight limitation in the manual.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: Category 4 requires compliance with the applicable approved operating limitations. General night lighting does not amend a daylight-only limitation.
Why A is incorrect: A general operational rule does not rewrite an aircraft-specific approved limitation.
Why C is incorrect: Category 4 relies on those limitations rather than overriding them.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.140 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.140

questions.prompt: A fixed-wing drone is above its usual wings-level stall speed when a sharp maneuver demands a high angle of attack. Can the wing still stall?

choices.A: No. Any speed above the reference guarantees attached airflow.
choices.B: Yes. Exceeding the critical angle of attack can stall the wing even above that reference speed.
choices.C: No. A stall occurs only after the motor stops.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: A stall follows exceeding the wing's critical angle of attack. A reference stall speed applies to a particular condition and does not guarantee protection during every maneuver.
Why A is incorrect: The maneuver can raise the required angle of attack and load factor.
Why C is incorrect: An aerodynamic wing stall is different from an engine or motor stoppage.
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, ch. 5, Aerodynamics of Flight — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak

questions.prompt: A Flight Service specialist provides a weather briefing and advises the crew to review controlled airspace at the site. The crew has no issued airspace authorization. Does receiving the briefing establish §107.41 authorization?

choices.A: Yes. Any FAA-related briefing automatically approves the planned airspace.
choices.B: Yes. A record of the briefing is equivalent to a LAANC approval.
choices.C: No. Obtain the applicable ATC authorization through the appropriate process.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: A briefing provides information. The separate ATC authorization requirement must also be satisfied when applicable.
Why A is incorrect: Providing aviation information does not itself grant the requested airspace use.
Why B is incorrect: A briefing record does not substitute for an issued authorization.
Reference: FAA AIM, §§4-1-3 and 4-1-9, Flight Service and traffic advisories — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap4_section_1.html
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.41 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.41
Reference: FAA, Part 107 Airspace Authorizations — https://www.faa.gov/uas/commercial_operators/part_107_airspace_authorizations

questions.prompt: A drone will release a lightweight marker toward an empty target. The predicted drop path first passes through an occupied work area, and wind could carry the marker into workers. Does the empty intended target alone satisfy the dropping rule?

choices.A: Yes. Only the intended point of impact matters.
choices.B: Yes. A lightweight object is automatically outside §107.23(b).
choices.C: No. The release must avoid an undue hazard along the actual drop path as well.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Section 107.23(b) concerns an undue hazard from dropping an object. The actual path and foreseeable effects matter in addition to the intended target.
Why A is incorrect: An empty target does not remove hazards before the object reaches it.
Why B is incorrect: The section does not establish a blanket exemption for objects described as lightweight.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.23 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.23

questions.prompt: A chart image and its scale bar are enlarged together. On the reproduced page, a 1-nautical-mile bar measures 4 cm and a route measures 10 cm. What route distance follows from that bar?

choices.A: 4 nautical miles.
choices.B: 2.5 nautical miles.
choices.C: 10 nautical miles.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: The route is 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 bar lengths. Each bar still represents 1 nautical mile when the map and bar are scaled together.
Why A is incorrect: The printed bar's length is a page measurement rather than the route's represented ground distance.
Why C is incorrect: Centimeters on a resized page are not automatically nautical miles.
Reference: FAA Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide, July 9, 2026, VFR Terms and Symbols — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav/digital_products/aero_guide/
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, ch. 16, Navigation — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak

questions.prompt: An emergency requires a Part 107 deviation and also damages another person's repairable property by $900. No one is injured. The FAA has not yet requested an emergency-deviation report. Which reporting duty already applies?

choices.A: Report the qualifying safety event within 10 calendar days. A written deviation report is separately owed if the FAA requests it.
choices.B: Wait for an FAA request before reporting any part of the event.
choices.C: The emergency deviation automatically removes the safety-event reporting duty.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The property damage triggers §107.9 independently. Section 107.21(b) makes the written deviation report dependent on a request.
Why B is incorrect: The safety-event provision has its own trigger and deadline.
Why C is incorrect: Emergency authority does not erase the separate reporting provision.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.9 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.9
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.21 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.21

questions.prompt: Two approved training setups have equal mass and draw a constant 100 watts. Pack A is 12 volts at 4 amp-hours, while Pack B is 24 volts at 3 amp-hours. Reserve 20 percent of each pack's nominal energy. Use watt-hours = volts × amp-hours. Which usable endurance estimate is correct?

choices.A: A gives about 34.6 minutes and B about 23.0 minutes.
choices.B: A gives about 23.0 minutes and B about 34.6 minutes.

questions.prompt: A standard Remote ID design proposal omits error correction because its test flights all occurred near the receiving device with a strong signal. Does that reasoning satisfy §89.310(e)?

choices.B: No. The equipment must incorporate error correction in the broadcast of the required message elements.
choices.C: Yes. Error correction is required only for a broadcast module, never for standard Remote ID.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: Section 89.310(e) expressly requires error correction. Favorable results in limited signal conditions do not remove that requirement.
Why A is incorrect: The rule does not condition the requirement on a particular field-test signal strength.

questions.prompt: Category 2 operating instructions list certain modifications that preserve eligibility. A proposed arm replacement is not on that list and has not otherwise been assessed. What should the pilot establish before a Category 2 flight with that arm?

choices.B: That any replacement fitting the same screw holes is automatically eligible.
choices.C: That the prior aircraft label alone authorizes every future modification.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The instructions identify modifications that preserve eligibility, while the preflight duty requires actual applicable eligibility. An unassessed change needs resolution.
Why B is incorrect: Mechanical fit alone does not establish the declared injury and safety characteristics.
Why C is incorrect: A label does not establish compliance after an arbitrary configuration change.

Why B is incorrect: Alder's total is within 12.0 pounds, but one mount carries 4.0 pounds and exceeds its local limit.

questions.prompt: The normal route lies above an empty private field. The programmed response to a control failure would carry the aircraft onto a busy road before landing. Which part of the plan needs attention?

Why C is incorrect: The loss-of-control duty explicitly reaches beyond the normal commanded route.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Section 107.49(d) applies when the small unmanned aircraft is powered. It does not limit the requirement to electric propulsion or a particular battery chemistry.

The fictional airport airspace panels in the written scenario data show two separate sites. At each, the drone would be 4,100 feet MSL and 300 feet AGL. Assume all other limits are met. At which site is the drone still inside the described airport airspace and therefore subject to §107.41 for that area?

Why C is incorrect: The minus sign excludes Q's stated Class D upper altitude.

questions.prompt: A waiver expressly permits the pilot to command two drones under stated conditions. One of the drones develops a known unsafe condition. Does the multiple-aircraft relief authorize completing its remaining route?

Why A is incorrect: A second aircraft's condition does not make the faulty aircraft safe.
Why B is incorrect: The stated relief concerns the number of aircraft, not arbitrary equipment failures.

questions.prompt: The dispatch screen shows 95% beside a controller icon and 26% beside an aircraft icon. The operator's procedure requires at least 80% aircraft battery at launch. Which reading governs that requirement?

questions.explanation:
Why B works: The requirement refers to the aircraft battery. The icon distinguishes that battery from the controller's separate supply.
Why A is incorrect: The largest displayed percentage is not automatically the aircraft's state of charge.
Why C is incorrect: The two batteries are separate supplies. Averaging their percentages does not establish aircraft energy.

questions.prompt: A drone hovers below a Class B shelf. A planned climb would enter that shelf while staying at exactly the same latitude and longitude. With no applicable authorization, what must the pilot account for?

choices.B: The climb crosses the vertical boundary into Class B even without lateral movement.
choices.C: A Class B shelf applies only to aircraft moving horizontally.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: Airspace has vertical as well as lateral limits. A climb can enter an overlying shelf without changing the plan-view point.
Why A is incorrect: Latitude and longitude do not specify altitude or the complete airspace position.
Why C is incorrect: A shelf's vertical volume applies to a hovering or climbing aircraft as well.

questions.prompt: A weather update gives sustained wind of 12 knots with gusts to 24 knots. The aircraft instructions prohibit launch when gusts exceed 20 knots. Which value controls this launch decision?

choices.A: The 18-knot average of sustained wind and gust, because the limit always uses an average.
choices.B: The 24-knot gust, which exceeds the stated limit.
choices.C: The 12-knot sustained value, because gusts do not count in aircraft instructions.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: The instructions explicitly specify gusts. The reported 24-knot gust exceeds that criterion even though sustained wind is lower.
Why A is incorrect: Averaging changes the criterion instead of applying the aircraft instructions.
Why C is incorrect: The stated criterion includes gusts rather than limiting the check to the sustained value.

questions.prompt: The crew's arming procedure requires the launch assistant to report “Hands clear.” The assistant is silent after moving behind the aircraft. What should the pilot do?

choices.A: Arm because moving behind the aircraft proves every person's hands are clear.

choices.C: Interpret silence as the required confirmation.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: The agreed procedure uses a positive confirmation. Position alone and silence do not establish that the check has been completed.
Why A is incorrect: One person's visible movement does not confirm the full condition the call is meant to verify.
Why C is incorrect: Silence can indicate a missed call or an unfinished task.

questions.prompt: A restricted circle has a 2.0-nautical-mile radius. The operator requires an additional 0.3-nautical-mile horizontal buffer outside it. Three straight candidate legs have verified closest distances from the circle's center of 2.2, 2.3, and 2.5 nautical miles. Which legs meet that stated buffer?

choices.A: The 2.3- and 2.5-nautical-mile legs.
choices.B: All three legs.
choices.C: Only the 2.5-nautical-mile leg.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The minimum acceptable closest distance is 2.0 + 0.3 = 2.3 NM. Equality meets the stated buffer, so the last two legs qualify.
Why B is incorrect: The 2.2-NM leg leaves only 0.2 NM outside the circle.
Why C is incorrect: A minimum of 2.3 includes a leg whose verified closest distance equals 2.3.

questions.prompt: An authorization limits the drone to 180 feet AGL. In the planned mode, the verified altitude error can put it 12 feet above the commanded height. Which of these setpoints accounts for that entire stated upward error without exceeding the ceiling?

questions.prompt: A drone damages a repairable equipment cart. The complete repair cost is $740, while its pre-event fair-market value was $300. The cart is not a total loss and there is no injury. Which amount applies to this §107.9 property-damage analysis?

choices.A: The $300 market value, which always replaces repair cost.
choices.B: The average of the two values, $520.
choices.C: The $740 repair cost, which exceeds $500.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: For repairable property, the rule's repair-cost branch includes labor and materials. The fair-market-value branch applies in the event of total loss.
Why A is incorrect: The facts explicitly identify a repairable item rather than a total loss.
Why B is incorrect: The regulation does not prescribe averaging repair cost and market value.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.9 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.9

questions.prompt:
Written scenario data: The chart's Mount Lemmon RCO box names Prescott as the associated Flight Service facility; other nearby boxes mention Tucson Approach and Davis-Monthan tower.

Which Flight Service facility is named with the Mount Lemmon RCO in the written scenario data?

choices.A: Davis-Monthan tower.
choices.B: Prescott.
choices.C: Tucson Approach.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: Prescott is printed in the RCO facility box beneath Mount Lemmon.
Why A is incorrect: The military tower is a different service from the RCO's named Flight Service facility.
Why C is incorrect: Tucson Approach appears in a separate contact note, not as the Flight Service facility named with this RCO.
Reference: FAA Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide, July 9, 2026, VFR Terms and Symbols — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav/digital_products/aero_guide/
Reference: FAA AIM, §§4-1-3 and 4-1-9, Flight Service and traffic advisories — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap4_section_1.html
Reference: FAA VFR Raster Charts, Sectionals and effective dates — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav/digital_products/vfr/

questions.prompt: For a night flight, a drone's steady red and green position lights can be seen from more than 3 statute miles. No flashing anti-collision light is installed and no waiver applies. Do the steady lights alone meet §107.29(a)(2)?

choices.A: No. The required anti-collision lighting must also have a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision.
choices.B: Yes. Red and green colors replace the flash requirement.
choices.C: Yes. Range alone is the only lighting criterion.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: Night lighting must satisfy both the visibility and flash requirements. Steady position lights do not establish the required anti-collision flash function.
Why B is incorrect: The rule does not substitute particular position-light colors for flashing anti-collision lighting.
Why C is incorrect: A sufficient range does not satisfy a missing flash requirement.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.29 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.29

questions.prompt: The kit contains a recovery card for a different aircraft model. Its emergency control sequence differs from the current model's instructions. What should be established before launch?

choices.A: The crew has and understands the current aircraft's applicable emergency procedure.
choices.B: The card is usable because both aircraft have four motors.
choices.C: The crew can improvise a matching sequence if a fault occurs.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: Emergency procedures depend on the system and controls involved. A model mismatch must be resolved before the card can be relied on.
Why B is incorrect: A shared number of motors does not establish identical control functions or procedures.
Why C is incorrect: Waiting for an emergency leaves the known procedure gap unresolved.
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak

questions.prompt: A technician says “Ready to arm,” then immediately discovers a tool still resting on the aircraft. The pilot has not armed yet. What communication is needed?

choices.A: A prompt, unambiguous stop call that cancels the ready status and identifies the tool hazard.
choices.B: A request to check the tool after takeoff because the first ready call is final.
choices.C: A quiet note for the postflight log without interrupting the pilot.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The earlier readiness call could trigger arming. Immediately withdrawing it prevents the pilot from acting on information now known to be wrong.
Why B is incorrect: A readiness call is not irreversible when a hazard is discovered.
Why C is incorrect: A later record does not stop the impending unsafe action.
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt: A supervised trainee is manipulating the controls. The remote PIC says only the remote PIC is legally required to comply with the §107.51 operating limits. Is that accurate?

choices.A: Yes. The trainee is covered only after obtaining a certificate.
choices.B: Yes. Direct supervision exempts the trainee from those limits.
choices.C: No. The section expressly applies to the remote PIC and the person manipulating the controls.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Section 107.51 names both roles. Supervision provides a pathway to manipulate controls without independent pilot qualification, not relief from operating limits.
Why A is incorrect: The role exists and carries applicable duties even when the trainee is uncertificated.
Why B is incorrect: The supervised pathway does not authorize violations of those limits.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.51 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.51

questions.prompt: A preflight alternate was an empty loading bay. During flight, a delivery truck occupies it and starts unloading. The primary pad remains clear, and the crew can recover there now. What should the remote PIC do?

choices.A: Continue to count the bay as available because it passed the preflight check.
choices.B: Assume the truck will leave before the drone needs to land.
choices.C: Reassess the alternate's loss and preserve a safe recovery plan using current conditions.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: An alternate must remain usable when needed. Its changed occupancy removes the earlier assumption and calls for a current recovery decision.
Why A is incorrect: A past inspection does not reserve an area against later occupation.
Why B is incorrect: An unconfirmed future departure does not establish a usable recovery site.
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
